A declaration of trust in Rhode Island is the written instrument that creates a trust. The settlor states an intent to hold property for named beneficiaries and appoints a trustee to manage it. The trust must be in writing, signed by the settlor, and delivered to the trustee with intent to create a trust. Rhode Island does not have comprehensive statutory trust execution requirements, relying heavily on common law. Notarization is recommended though not required by the trust statute itself. The trust becomes active when it is funded: real property moves by a new deed to the trustee, and bank and brokerage accounts are retitled in the name of the trust or trustee. faq.a: No. Rhode Island has not adopted the Uniform Trust Code and does not have a general UTC-style certification of trust statute. The closest analog is R.I. Gen. faq.q: Does a Rhode Island declaration of trust have to be notarized or witnessed?
faq.a: Rhode Island does not have statutory trust execution requirements comparable to UTC states. The trust must be in writing, signed by the settlor, and delivered to the trustee. Notarization is recommended though not required by the trust statute itself. R.I. Gen. Laws Â§ 34-4-27 itself states no oath, acknowledgment, witness, notary, or attorney authentication requirement for the memorandum of trust. For real property transactions, the memorandum or trust instrument must be recorded. Rhode Island permits remote online notarization.

faq.q: Can a Rhode Island trust continue forever?
faq.a: Yes. The Rhode Island General Assembly repealed the Rule Against Perpetuities in 1999, allowing perpetual trusts and dynasty trusts. This was a significant reform making Rhode Island one of the earlier states to abolish the RAP. The specific terms of the trust instrument and how the trust is administered still determine what happens in any particular case. Rhode Island's reliance on common law rather than a comprehensive code means that trust duration is governed by judicial interpretation and the general principles of equitable trust law.

faq.q: How does Rhode Island handle third-party reliance on trust documents?
faq.a: Rhode Island relies on the common law safeguarding provisions of R.I. Gen. Laws Â§ 18-3-3, which protects persons dealing with trustees. Third parties without actual contrary knowledge may rely on the statements in a memorandum of trust under Â§ 34-4-27. Unlike UTC states, Rhode Island does not have a general transaction-enforcement or bad-faith-demand damages rule in its trust certification provisions. The reliance protection is limited to third parties without actual contrary knowledge, without the additional enforcement and bad-faith-demand provisions found in the UTC model. blocks.common_mistakes: Common issues include assuming Rhode Island has a UTC-style certification of trust statute (it does not), and confusing the real-property memorandum under Â§ 34-4-27 with a general certification of trust. The memorandum requires attachment of relevant trust provisions regarding real estate authority, which is more detailed than the UTC certification model. People also overlook the all-or-all signer requirement: the memorandum must be executed by every settlor or every current trustee, which is stricter than the UTC's any-trustee rule. Another frequent mix-up is assuming Rhode Island's reliance protection includes the UTC's bad-faith-demand damages provisions, but Â§ 18-3-3 does not provide the same level of protection. Rhode Island's higher fiduciary income tax rates compared to neighboring states are also frequently overlooked in trust situs planning. The common law framework provides flexibility but less statutory certainty and guidance for trustees and beneficiaries.
blocks.state_notes: Rhode Island operates under R.I. Gen. Laws Title 18 (Fiduciaries), relying on common law and scattered statutory provisions rather than a comprehensive trust code. Rhode Island has NOT adopted the Uniform Trust Code, making its trust law less codified and more dependent on judicial precedent than most other states. The closest analog to a certification of trust is R.I. Gen. Laws Â§ 34-4-27, which provides a real-property affidavit or memorandum of trust, not a general certification of trust. Rhode Island repealed the Rule Against Perpetuities in 1999, allowing perpetual trusts and dynasty trusts. The state repealed the centuries-old law prohibiting property owners from shielding assets in a trust from creditors in 1999. Rhode Island imposes state income tax on trust income for resident trusts at rates of 3.75% to 5.99%. The state has no state estate tax.
